paragraphs: After studying the pages of history and viewing the living world with anxious concern, I have been weighed down by the most melancholy feelings of sorrowful indignation, and I have sighed when forced to admit either that nature has made a great difference between one man and another, or that the civilization the world has so far achieved has been very partial. I have looked through various books written on education, and I have patiently observed how parents behave and how schools are run; but what has been the result? A deep conviction that the neglected education of my fellow creatures is the chief source of the misery I lament, and that women in particular are made weak and wretched by a number of converging causes, all springing from one hasty conclusion. The conduct and manners of women plainly prove, in fact, that their minds are not in a healthy state. Like flowers planted in soil that is too rich, they sacrifice strength and usefulness to beauty; and the showy leaves, after pleasing a fastidious eye, wither unnoticed on the stalk long before the season when they should have reached maturity. One cause of this barren blooming I attribute to a false system of education, taken from the books on this subject written by men who, regarding females as women rather than as human creatures, have been more eager to make them alluring mistresses than rational wives. And the understanding of the sex has been so deceived by this hollow homage that the civilized women of this century, with a few exceptions, are anxious only to inspire love, when they ought to cherish a nobler ambition and command respect by their abilities and virtues.

In a treatise on the rights and manners of women, therefore, the works written specifically for their improvement must not be overlooked — especially when the claim is made in plain terms that women’s minds are weakened by false refinement; that the books of instruction written by men of genius have had the same effect as more frivolous works; and that, in the true Mahometan style, women are regarded only as females and not as part of the human species, even though improvable reason is admitted to be the dignified distinction that raises men above the animal creation and puts a natural sceptre in a feeble hand.

Yet I would not have my readers suppose, because I am a woman, that I intend to stir up violently the disputed question of the equality or inferiority of the sex. But since the subject lies in my path, and I cannot pass over it without exposing the main drift of my reasoning to misinterpretation, I shall pause for a moment to give my opinion in a few words. In the government of the physical world, it can be observed that the female is, in general, inferior to the male. The male pursues, the female yields — this is the law of nature, and it does not appear to be suspended or repealed in favour of woman. This physical superiority cannot be denied — and it is a noble prerogative! But not content with this natural pre-eminence, men try to sink us still lower, merely to make us alluring objects for a moment; and women, intoxicated by the adoration that men pay them under the sway of their senses, do not try to win a lasting place in men’s hearts, or to become the friends of the fellow creatures who find amusement in their company.

I can foresee an obvious objection. From every quarter I have heard outcries against masculine women; but where are they to be found? If men use this label to attack women’s enthusiasm for hunting, shooting and gambling, I shall join the outcry most heartily; but if it is aimed at the imitation of manly virtues, or, more properly speaking, at the attainment of those talents and virtues whose exercise ennobles the human character, and which raise females in the scale of animal being when they are included under the general term mankind — then all who view women with a philosophical eye must, I should think, wish with me that they may grow more and more masculine every day.

This discussion naturally divides the subject. I shall first consider women in the broad light of human creatures who, like men, are placed on this earth to develop their faculties; and afterwards I shall point out more particularly their own special calling.

I also wish to avoid an error into which many respectable writers have fallen, for the instruction so far addressed to women has been better suited to LADIES, if we except the little indirect advice scattered through Sandford and Merton. Addressing my sex in a firmer tone, however, I pay particular attention to those in the middle class, because they seem to be in the most natural state. Perhaps the seeds of false refinement, immorality and vanity have always been scattered by the great. Weak, artificial beings, lifted prematurely and unnaturally above the common needs and affections of their kind, undermine the very foundation of virtue and spread corruption through the whole mass of society! As a class of mankind, they have the strongest claim to pity! The education of the rich tends to make them vain and helpless, and the developing mind is not strengthened by the practice of those duties that give dignity to human character. They live only to amuse themselves, and by the same law that in nature invariably produces certain effects, they soon provide nothing but barren amusement.

But as I intend to look separately at the different ranks of society and at the moral character of women in each, this hint is enough for now; I have mentioned the subject only because it seems to me the very essence of an introduction to give a brief account of the contents of the work it introduces.

My own sex will, I hope, forgive me if I treat them as rational creatures instead of flattering their FASCINATING graces and regarding them as if they were in a state of perpetual childhood, unable to stand on their own. I earnestly wish to show what true dignity and human happiness consist in. I wish to persuade women to try to acquire strength of both mind and body, and to convince them that the soft phrases — susceptibility of heart, delicacy of sentiment and refinement of taste — are almost synonymous with terms for weakness, and that beings who are only the objects of pity, and of that kind of love which has been called its sister, will soon become objects of contempt.

Setting aside, then, those pretty feminine phrases that men condescendingly use to soften our slavish dependence, and scorning that weak elegance of mind, exquisite sensibility and sweet docility of manner supposed to be the sexual characteristics of the weaker vessel, I wish to show that elegance is inferior to virtue; that the first aim of worthy ambition is to earn a character as a human being, regardless of the distinction of sex; and that lesser aims should be tested against this simple touchstone.

This is a rough sketch of my plan; and if I express my conviction with the strong emotions I feel whenever I think of the subject, some of my readers will feel the force of what experience and reflection dictate. Inspired by this important aim, I shall disdain to pick my phrases or polish my style — I aim to be useful, and sincerity will keep me unaffected. Since I would rather persuade by the force of my arguments than dazzle by the elegance of my language, I shall not waste my time in rounding off sentences or in manufacturing the swollen bombast of artificial feelings, which, coming from the head, never reach the heart. I shall concern myself with things, not words! And, anxious to make my sex more respectable members of society, I shall try to avoid the flowery diction that has slid from essays into novels, and from novels into everyday letters and conversation.

These pretty nothings, these caricatures of the real beauty of sensibility, rolling glibly off the tongue, corrupt the taste and create a kind of sickly delicacy that turns away from plain, unadorned truth; and a flood of false sentiments and overstrained feelings, stifling the natural emotions of the heart, makes insipid those domestic pleasures that ought to sweeten the performance of the stern duties which educate a rational and immortal being for a nobler field of action.

The education of women has recently received more attention than it used to; yet women are still considered a frivolous sex, and are ridiculed or pitied by the writers who try to improve them through satire or instruction. It is admitted that they spend many of their early years acquiring a smattering of accomplishments, while strength of body and mind is sacrificed to libertine notions of beauty and to the desire to settle themselves in life by the only means through which women can rise in the world — marriage. And since this desire turns them into mere animals, when they marry they behave as such children may be expected to behave: they dress up, they paint their faces, and they nickname God’s creatures. Surely these weak beings are fit only for the harem! Can they manage a household, or look after the poor babies they bring into the world?

If, then, it can fairly be inferred from the present conduct of the sex, and from the prevailing love of pleasure that takes the place of ambition and of those nobler passions that open and enlarge the soul, that the instruction women have received has only tended, along with the constitution of civil society, to make them insignificant objects of desire — mere breeders of fools! — and if it can be proved that, in the attempt to give them accomplishments without cultivating their understanding, they are taken out of their sphere of duties and made ridiculous and useless once the short-lived bloom of beauty is over*, then I presume that RATIONAL men will excuse me for trying to persuade women to become more masculine and respectable.
(*Footnote. A lively writer, whose name I cannot remember, asks what business women over forty have in the world.)

Indeed, the word masculine is only a bogeyman. There is little reason to fear that women will acquire too much courage or fortitude, for their apparent inferiority in bodily strength must make them, to some degree, dependent on men in the various relationships of life. But why should this dependence be increased by prejudices that give virtue a sex and confuse simple truths with sensual daydreams?

Women are, in fact, so degraded by mistaken notions of female excellence that I do not mean to add a paradox when I assert that this artificial weakness produces a tendency to tyrannize and gives birth to cunning, the natural opponent of strength, which leads them to put on those contemptible childish airs that undermine esteem even while they arouse desire. Stop fostering these prejudices, and women will naturally settle into their subordinate, yet respectable, place in life.

It hardly seems necessary to say that I am now speaking of the sex in general. Many individual women have more sense than their male relatives; and since nothing tips the scale where there is a constant struggle for balance unless it naturally has more weight, some women govern their husbands without degrading themselves, because intellect will always govern.
